```{r setup}
#| include: false

# Load required packages
library(here)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(sf)
library(plotly)
library(leaflet)
library(DT)
library(knitr)
library(kableExtra)

# Set paths relative to this article's location (in blog/Gbif Kenya/docs/)
results_dir <- here("blog", "Gbif Kenya", "results")

# Alternative: use relative path from docs folder
# results_dir <- "../results"

# Load pre-computed results
spatial_grid <- readRDS(file.path(results_dir, "spatial_bias", "spatial_grid_effort.rds"))
env_comparison <- readRDS(file.path(results_dir, "spatial_bias", "environmental_comparison.rds"))
taxonomic_summary <- readRDS(file.path(results_dir, "taxonomic_bias", "taxonomic_bias_summary.rds"))
class_summary <- readRDS(file.path(results_dir, "taxonomic_bias", "class_summary.rds"))
quality_assessment <- readRDS(file.path(results_dir, "data_quality", "data_quality_assessment.rds"))
```

I set out to understand Kenya's biodiversity data. What I discovered was a mirror reflecting how we do science itself.
Kenya hosts extraordinary biodiversity — from montane forests to coral reefs, from the Maasai Mara's megafauna to thousands of endemic species found nowhere else. But when I downloaded 4.9 million occurrence records from [GBIF](https://www.gbif.org/) to assess what we actually *know*, the picture that emerged was humbling.

## Discovery 1: We've barely scratched the surface

Only **13.3%** of Kenya's land area contains any recorded biodiversity observations.

Let that sink in. Despite decades of research, expeditions, and citizen science, 86.7% of the country — nearly 500,000 km² — has zero occurrence records in the world's largest biodiversity database.

The arid and semi-arid lands covering over 80% of Kenya? Drastically undersampled. Northern Kenya's unique ecosystems? Virtually invisible. Coastal zones and high-altitude peaks? Significant gaps.

Our biodiversity maps may actually be maps of **where researchers travel**, not where species live.

### Interactive Map: Where We've Actually Sampled

Explore the map below to see sampling effort across Kenya. Click on cells to see detailed statistics. Notice how sampling clusters around major cities and along accessible routes.

```{r sampling-map}
#| fig-cap: "Interactive map of sampling effort across Kenya. Hexagonal cells (~10 km resolution) show the number of occurrence records. Click cells for details."

# Transform to WGS84 for leaflet
spatial_grid_wgs84 <- st_transform(spatial_grid, 4326)

# Create color palette for record counts (log scale)
pal <- colorNumeric(
  palette = "viridis",
  domain = log10(spatial_grid_wgs84$n_records + 1),
  na.color = "transparent"
)

# Create interactive map
leaflet(spatial_grid_wgs84) %>%
  addProviderTiles("OpenStreetMap") %>%
  addPolygons(
    fillColor = ~pal(log10(n_records + 1)),
    fillOpacity = 0.6,
    color = "white",
    weight = 0.8,
    popup = ~paste0(
      "<strong>Grid Cell Summary</strong><br>",
      "Records: ", format(n_records, big.mark = ","), "<br>",
      "Species: ", n_species, "<br>",
      "Log10 Records: ", round(log10(n_records + 1), 2)
    ),
    highlightOptions = highlightOptions(
      weight = 2,
      color = "#666",
      fillOpacity = 0.8,
      bringToFront = TRUE
    )
  ) %>%
  addLegend(
    pal = pal,
    values = ~log10(n_records + 1),
    title = "Log10(Records)",
    position = "bottomright",
    opacity = 0.7
  ) %>%
  addControl(
    html = "<div style='background: white; padding: 10px; border-radius: 5px;'>
      <strong>Sampling Effort Map</strong><br>
      <small>• Zoom to explore regions<br>
      • Click cells for statistics<br>
      • Note clustering near cities</small>
    </div>",
    position = "topright"
  )
```

## Discovery 2: "Biodiversity data" is really bird data

When I calculated taxonomic representation, one number stopped me cold: **87.5%**.

That's the proportion of all Kenya's GBIF records belonging to a single class — Aves (birds). The Gini coefficient measuring taxonomic inequality came out at **0.966**, indicating extreme concentration.

Birds are magnificent and deserve study. But Kenya's insects, fungi, soil microbes, marine invertebrates, and countless other groups collectively comprise far more of actual biodiversity. They're nearly absent from the data.

We're not measuring Kenya's biodiversity. We're measuring what humans find **charismatic and convenient** to observe.

### Interactive Treemap: What We've Actually Recorded

The size of each box represents the number of records. Hover to see details.

```{r taxonomic-treemap}
#| fig-cap: "Taxonomic representation in Kenya's GBIF data. Box size = number of records. Aves (birds) dominates with 87.5% of all records."

top_15_classes <- head(class_summary, 15)

fig_treemap <- plot_ly(
  data = top_15_classes,
  type = "treemap",
  labels = ~class,
  parents = rep("", nrow(top_15_classes)),
  values = ~n_records,
  marker = list(
    colors = ~n_species,
    colorscale = 'Viridis',
    colorbar = list(title = "Species Count")
  ),
  text = ~paste0(
    "<b>", class, "</b><br>",
    "Kingdom: ", kingdom, "<br>",
    "Records: ", format(n_records, big.mark = ","), "<br>",
    "Species: ", format(n_species, big.mark = ","), "<br>",
    "Families: ", n_families
  ),
  hovertemplate = '%{text}<extra></extra>',
  textposition = "middle center",
  pathbar = list(visible = FALSE)
) %>%
  layout(
    title = list(
      text = "Taxonomic Representation (Top 15 Classes)",
      font = list(size = 16)
    ),
    margin = list(l = 0, r = 0, t = 50, b = 0)
  )

fig_treemap
```

```{r top-classes-table}
#| tbl-cap: "Top 10 taxonomic classes by number of records"

top_10_display <- head(class_summary, 10) %>%
  mutate(
    `% of Total` = sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * n_records / sum(class_summary$n_records))
  ) %>%
  select(Kingdom = kingdom, Phylum = phylum, Class = class,
         Records = n_records, Species = n_species, `% of Total`)

datatable(
  top_10_display,
  options = list(
    pageLength = 10,
    dom = 't',
    ordering = FALSE
  ),
  rownames = FALSE,
  class = 'cell-border stripe hover'
) %>%
  formatCurrency('Records', currency = '', digits = 0, mark = ',') %>%
  formatCurrency('Species', currency = '', digits = 0, mark = ',')
```

## Discovery 3: More than half the data has quality issues

**54.7%** of records carried at least one quality flag.

Duplicates accounted for 42.5% — the same observation submitted through multiple data pathways. Coordinate issues affected 12.9%, including records mysteriously placed at country centroids or capital cities (a telltale sign of imprecise georeferencing). Nearly 7% lacked species-level identification.

This isn't a criticism of data collectors. It reflects the realities of aggregating data across institutions, decades, and methodologies. But it means we cannot treat these records as uniformly reliable.

## Discovery 4: Environmental bias is systematic

I compared the environmental conditions at sampled locations against Kenya's full environmental space. Every variable — elevation, temperature, precipitation — showed **statistically significant bias**.

Sampling concentrates in mid-elevation, moderate-climate areas near cities and roads. The environmental extremes — hot lowlands, wet forests, alpine zones — are underrepresented.

### Interactive Comparison: Sampled vs Available Environments

```{r environmental-bias}
#| fig-cap: "Environmental bias assessment. Red = sampled locations, Grey = available environmental space across Kenya. Significant divergence indicates systematic sampling bias."
#| fig-height: 8

# Prepare data for plotly
env_long <- env_comparison %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = c(elevation, temperature, precipitation),
               names_to = "variable", values_to = "value") %>%
  filter(!is.na(value)) %>%
  mutate(
    variable_label = case_when(
      variable == "elevation" ~ "Elevation (m)",
      variable == "temperature" ~ "Mean Annual Temperature (°C × 10)",
      variable == "precipitation" ~ "Annual Precipitation (mm)"
    ),
    type_label = ifelse(type == "sampled", "Sampled Locations", "Available Space")
  )

# Create interactive plotly density plots
plot_list <- list()

for (var in c("elevation", "temperature", "precipitation")) {
  var_data <- env_long %>% filter(variable == var)
  var_label <- unique(var_data$variable_label)
  
  sampled_data <- var_data %>% filter(type == "sampled") %>% pull(value)
  available_data <- var_data %>% filter(type == "available") %>% pull(value)
  
  fig <- plot_ly() %>%
    add_trace(
      x = density(available_data)$x,
      y = density(available_data)$y,
      type = 'scatter',
      mode = 'lines',
      name = 'Available Space',
      fill = 'tozeroy',
      fillcolor = 'rgba(128, 128, 128, 0.4)',
      line = list(color = 'rgb(128, 128, 128)', width = 2),
      hovertemplate = paste0('<b>Available Space</b><br>',
                             var_label, ': %{x:.1f}<br>',
                             'Density: %{y:.4f}<extra></extra>')
    ) %>%
    add_trace(
      x = density(sampled_data)$x,
      y = density(sampled_data)$y,
      type = 'scatter',
      mode = 'lines',
      name = 'Sampled Locations',
      fill = 'tozeroy',
      fillcolor = 'rgba(255, 0, 0, 0.4)',
      line = list(color = 'rgb(255, 0, 0)', width = 2),
      hovertemplate = paste0('<b>Sampled Locations</b><br>',
                             var_label, ': %{x:.1f}<br>',
                             'Density: %{y:.4f}<extra></extra>')
    ) %>%
    layout(
      title = list(text = var_label, font = list(size = 14)),
      xaxis = list(title = var_label),
      yaxis = list(title = "Density"),
      hovermode = 'closest',
      showlegend = TRUE,
      legend = list(x = 0.7, y = 0.95)
    )
  
  plot_list[[var]] <- fig
}

# Combine plots vertically
subplot(plot_list, nrows = 3, shareX = FALSE, titleY = TRUE, margin = 0.08) %>%
  layout(
    title = list(
      text = "Environmental Bias: Sampled vs Available Space",
      font = list(size = 16, color = '#333')
    ),
    showlegend = TRUE,
    height = 700
  )
```

## What This Means for Kenya

These findings aren't cause for despair. They're a **roadmap**.

**The gaps are now mapped.** We know precisely which regions and taxa need attention. Future sampling can be strategic rather than opportunistic.

**The biases are quantified.** Researchers can incorporate bias corrections into models. Conservation planners can distinguish between "species absent" and "species unsampled."

**A baseline exists.** Kenya's Environment Institute, conservation organisations, and research institutions now have documented metrics to measure progress against.

**Opportunities abound.** Citizen science programmes can target undersampled areas. University research can prioritise neglected taxa. International collaborations can address the data gaps systematically.

## The Bigger Picture

Kenya isn't unique. These patterns — accessibility bias, taxonomic bias, environmental bias — appear in biodiversity data globally. What differs is whether we acknowledge and quantify them honestly.

I built this analysis to be **fully reproducible**. Every statistic traces to source code. The methodology transfers to any country, any taxonomic group, any observational dataset. Because transparent, reproducible science is how we move from data to knowledge.

Kenya's biodiversity is far richer than our current data reflects. Admitting what we don't know is the first step toward knowing more.
